entry.title: Neutrino Hunters: Searching for Ghostly Particles in Antarctic Ice, with Abigail Vieregg

media:group.media:title: Neutrino Hunters: Searching for Ghostly Particles in Antarctic Ice, with Abigail Vieregg
media:group.media:description:
Deep beneath the ice of Antarctica and high above its frozen expanse, University of Chicago astrophysicist Abby Vieregg is hunting for neutrinos—some of the most elusive particles in the universe. Often called "ghost particles," these tiny messengers travel across billions of light-years, passing right through ordinary matter unnoticed. She is among the many scientists hunting for high-energy neutrinos—an area of research that was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.
In this episode, Vieregg discusses how her team designs and launches cutting-edge radio detectors—from high-altitude NASA balloons over the South Pole to massive ice-drilling arrays in Greenland. She explains what these mysterious cosmic signals can teach us about black holes, exploding stars, and the fundamental laws of physics governing our universe.

entry.title: Recreating A Sense of Touch, Using Our Minds, with Nicholas Hatsopoulos

media:group.media:title: Recreating A Sense of Touch, Using Our Minds, with Nicholas Hatsopoulos
media:group.media:description:
What if your thoughts could allow you to feel the texture of an object, type a message or move a robotic arm? How does the brain translate thought into physical movement, and can technology bridge the gap for paralyzed patients, whose pathways are broken?
University of Chicago neuroscientist Nicholas Hatsopoulos is transforming that fundamental neuroscience into life-changing medical technology. By implanting microelectrode arrays directly into the brain, his team decodes the neural patterns that fire when a person intends to move. This brain-machine interface technology is allowing patients who are paralyzed or have ALS the ability to control robotic limbs, reach for objects, and regain touch sensation through their thoughts.

entry.title: Why The Key to Treating Cancer May Be In Your Gut, with Thomas Gajewski

media:group.media:title: Why The Key to Treating Cancer May Be In Your Gut, with Thomas Gajewski
media:group.media:description:
For decades, traditional cancer treatments like chemotherapy and radiation have targeted tumors directly—often with severe side effects and mixed results. But what if the key to treating cancer was already inside our bodies?
Prof. Thomas Gajewski, a renowned oncologist at the University of Chicago, is leading a revolution by using the body’s gut microbiome to fight cancer. His pioneering work in cancer immunotherapy focuses on why some patients with melanoma responded dramatically to immune-based therapies while others do not. In this episode, Gajewski discusses how training T-cells to recognize and attack tumors is transforming oncology, why the microbiome might hold the key to supercharging cancer treatments, and what it will take to make life-saving immunotherapies effective for every patient.

entry.title: The Little-Known Secrets To A Good Life, with Shigehiro Oishi

media:group.media:title: The Little-Known Secrets To A Good Life, with Shigehiro Oishi
media:group.media:description:
What makes a good life? For decades, psychologists have debated whether true fulfillment comes from happiness—a life of comfort and joy—or meaning—a life of purpose and impact. But what if there's a third way?
University of Chicago psychology professor Shigehiro Oishi has spent his career studying happiness, meaning, and what truly brings people deep satisfaction. His new research suggests that some of the most fulfilled people don’t prioritize either—they live psychologically rich lives, full of novelty, challenges, and transformative experiences. In this episode, Oishi explains why psychological richness might be the missing piece in our search for fulfillment.

entry.title: Anthropologist Ryan Cecil Jobson on what the Caribbean can tell us about the world

media:group.media:title: Anthropologist Ryan Cecil Jobson on what the Caribbean can tell us about the world
media:group.media:description:
What can a small island nation reveal about oil, power and the legacy of colonialism?
As an anthropologist of the Caribbean at the University of Chicago, Ryan Cecil Jobson argues that small places hold big insights. His book The Petro-state Masquerade: Oil, Sovereignty, and Power in Trinidad and Tobago explores the relationship between fossil fuel extraction, political power, and post-colonial national identity.
Jobson also follows in the tradition of the late UChicago anthropologist Michel-Rolph Trouillot— a professor, musician, Haitian, and political dissident—whose field-shaping work moved the Caribbean from the margins to the global center stage.
For the first time, Trouillot’s papers and archives are on public display in an exhibition co-curated by Jobson. “History on the Edges: Michel-Rolph Trouillot's Caribbean” is on view at the Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center Gallery at the Regenstein Library through Aug. 21, 2026.
View the web exhibition: https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/collex/exhibits/history-on-the-edges-michel-rolph-trouillots-caribbean/

entry.title: UChicago Prof. Yu Deng receives Fields Medal, highest honor in mathematics

media:group.media:title: UChicago Prof. Yu Deng receives Fields Medal, highest honor in mathematics
media:group.media:description:
The Fields Medal is awarded every four years to recognize outstanding mathematical achievement. Deng and collaborators were honored for addressing one of a famous set of problems laid out more than 125 years ago—mathematically connecting the equations governing the motion of gases from the smallest to the largest scales.
Deng is the 11th current or former UChicago mathematician to become a Fields medalist. Read more at news.uchicago.edu

entry.title: How to Use Nature to Restore Your Focus, with Marc Berman

media:group.media:title: How to Use Nature to Restore Your Focus, with Marc Berman
media:group.media:description:
What if the secret to restoring your focus, improving your mental health, and even reducing crime rates wasn’t found in an app or a pill, but in a tree? In this episode, we speak with University of Chicago psychologist Marc Berman, whose research on “soft fascination” and nature’s cognitive effects is reshaping how we think about everything from urban planning to depression treatment. From groundbreaking hospital studies to surprising results with plastic plants, Berman’s work uncovers the deep—and often invisible—power that natural environments hold over our minds and bodies. Whether you're a city planner, a parent, or just someone feeling mentally fatigued, this conversation may just change the way you think about a walk in the park.

entry.title: What Our Trash Problem Says About Our Culture, with Sarah Newman

media:group.media:title: What Our Trash Problem Says About Our Culture, with Sarah Newman
media:group.media:description:
Every day, we throw things away, only to be forgotten forever. But society didn’t always work in the same way. In this episode, we speak with University of Chicago scholar and anthropologist Sarah Newman to discuss her book, Unmaking Waste: New Histories of Old Things.
An archaeologist by training, Newman discusses the history of trash across time—from the ancient Mayan civilization through today’s disposable culture. She argues that other societies valued objects much more deeply, reusing and recycling items in innovative ways. But will we ever return to this kind of zero-waste mentality? Newman argues that true sustainability requires a radical, systemic overhaul of how products are designed, valued and dismantled. She challenges us to look beyond the recycling bin and imagine a world where waste isn't just managed, but systematically unmade if we are to genuinely rethink our relationship with garbage and reshape our future. entry.title: How Websites Trick You Using ‘Dark Patterns’ with Marshini Chetty

media:group.media:title: How Websites Trick You Using ‘Dark Patterns’ with Marshini Chetty
media:group.media:description:
Why does it seem so difficult to cancel an online subscription, delete an account, or opt out of data tracking? You might think it’s just bad luck or a confusing online interface, but more often than not, it’s by design.
In this episode of Big Brains, we speak with Marshini Chetty, Professor in the University of Chicago’s Department of Computer Science. As a leading expert in human-computer interaction, Chetty reveals the science behind "dark patterns” online—the subtle, manipulative design choices woven into the apps and websites we use every day. We explore how these deceptive interfaces weaponize human psychology to keep us clicking, spending and sharing our data.

entry.title: A Big Brains/1440 event: Quantum technology

media:group.media:title: A Big Brains/1440 event: Quantum technology
media:group.media:description:
A recent event at the University of Chicago, hosted by Big Brains in partnership with 1440, sought to demystify quantum, separate the hype from reality and explore how it could transform our daily lives.
Three renowned UChicago scientists and engineers—Prof. David Awschalom, Fred Chong and Nadya Mason—discussed how UChicago was leading innovative research, in partnership with its affiliated labs Argonne and Fermilab, as well as other universities across the Midwest. They explained how quantum has the potential to revolutionize our world—from creating unhackable communications to supercharging quantum computers to detecting disease at the cellular level. They discussed the challenges as well as the opportunities, especially for the next generation of quantum engineers and scientists needed to make these dreams a reality.
Sony Kassam, editor-in-chief of 1440, served as emcee for the event, which also included a Q&A with audience members at the David Rubenstein Forum, who asked the UChicago scientists wide-ranging questions—including how they became interested in the field, their favorite quantum movies and shows, and how quantum will help humans reach their potential.
